newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Red Army members detained in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Japan Red Army members detained in Lebanon.

text.p: Lebanese authorities have arrested up to six key members of Japan's notorious Red Army guerrilla group, including a gunman involved in the 1972 Lod airport massacre, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Tuesday.

Hashimoto told reporters he had been informed by Lebanese officials that the ageing guerrillas and three supporters, all of them Japanese, were captured in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, where they had been holed up for years.
"We have the information. I believe it's five or six people, though I"m not sure," Hashimoto said.
Lebanese officials said the detainees included Kozo Okamoto, 49, who was involved in the May 1972 shootout at Tel Aviv's Lod airport in which 24 people died and 100 were injured.
Okamoto was captured by Israeli forces and sentenced to life imprisonment but was released in a Palestinian-Israeli prisoner exchange in May 1985.
Japanese media reports have named another four of the detained guerrillas as Kazuo Tohira, 44, Hisashi Matsuda, 48, Mariko Yamamoto, 56, and Masao Adachi, 57.
The Foreign Ministry would not comment on the number of guerrillas arrested, and the identity of the possible sixth member of the group to be detained was unclear.

Tohira, an expert forger of documents for the Red Army, and Matsuda, who was in jail for bank robbery, were both released in August 1975 in exchange for the release of hostages held at the United States consulate in Kuala Lumpur.
Tohira was later implicated in the September 1977 hijacking of a Japan Airlines plane in Dhaka.
Yamamoto and Adachi are wanted for forgery and other crimes.
The three supporters, two men and a woman, were not linked to any known crimes.
Home Affairs Minister Katsuhiko Shirakawa said Japan would wait for the result of Lebanese action against the group before deciding whether to apply for their extradition.
"Since the detention was made according to domestic laws, the Lebanese government has the right to take necessary measures first," Shirakawa told a news conference.
The Japanese Red Army, founded in 1971, has about 40 members operating mainly in Lebanon and allied to hardline Palestinian factions.
Red Army leader Fusako Shigenobu, 51, is still at large and is high on the international wanted list.
